language_wrapper: Consider the family of integrals I_n = ∫_0^{pi/2} [sin^2({frequency_multiplier}·n·t)] / (sin t)^{ {exponent_q} } dt. Define the scaling S_n as follows: if {exponent_q} ≠ 1 then S_n = n^{ {exponent_q} − 1}, and if {exponent_q} = 1 then S_n = log base {log_base} of n. Determine the greatest integer less than {scale_factor} × lim_{n→∞} (I_n / S_n).
hardness_rationale: The seed problem uses the borderline case q=1, where the singularity at t=0 yields a logarithmic divergence and the asymptotic constant is straightforward once one recognizes sin^2(nt) = (1 − cos(2nt))/2 and applies log growth. Our generalized family replaces csc(t) with csc^q(t) for a real q in (0,2) and introduces a frequency multiplier, requiring the solver to distinguish between two regimes: (i) a delicate logarithmic case at q=1 with base-dependent scaling, and (ii) polynomial growth cases q≠1, which demand asymptotic analysis of oscillatory integrals via substitution and knowledge of the classic integral ∫_0^∞ (1−cos u) u^{-q} du = Γ(1−q) cos(π q/2). This elevates the difficulty by introducing special-function constants (Gamma and trigonometric factors), subtle handling of singular behavior, and careful scaling by n^{q−1}, significantly beyond the direct averaging techniques sufficient for the seed.
notes: Proof sketch: Write sin^2({frequency_multiplier} n t) = (1 − cos(2 {frequency_multiplier} n t))/2. For q in (0,2), the integral I_n is dominated by the neighborhood of t=0, where sin t ~ t. Split the integral at a small fixed epsilon. On [epsilon, pi/2], the integrand is bounded and contributes O(1), independent of n. On (0, epsilon), replace (sin t)^{q} by t^{q}(1 + O(t^2)), yielding I_n = (1/2) ∫_0^{epsilon} (1 − cos(2 {frequency_multiplier} n t)) t^{-q} dt + O(1). With u = 2 {frequency_multiplier} n t, we get I_n = (1/2) (2 {frequency_multiplier} n)^{q−1} ∫_0^{2 {frequency_multiplier} n epsilon} (1 − cos u) u^{-q} du + O(1). For q≠1, the improper integral ∫_0^{∞} (1 − cos u) u^{-q} du converges for q∈(0,2)\{1} and equals Γ(1−q) cos(π q/2). Hence lim_{n→∞} I_n / n^{q−1} = (1/2) (2 {frequency_multiplier})^{q−1} Γ(1−q) cos(π q/2). For q=1, the integral over (0, epsilon) is ∫_0^{epsilon} (1 − cos(2 {frequency_multiplier} n t)) / t dt = log(2 {frequency_multiplier} n) + C + o(1), by the classical asymptotic ∫_0^{X} (1 − cos u)/u du = log X + γ + o(1). Thus I_n ~ (1/2) log(2 {frequency_multiplier} n) + O(1), so I_n / log_base(n) → (1/2) ln({log_base}), independent of {frequency_multiplier}. These limits are positive, ensuring the requested floor is well-defined. The generator ensures q lies in (0,2) and avoids the pole at q=1 when using polynomial scaling; the verifier recomputes the limit and enforces nontrivial magnitude to prevent trivial instances.
source_question: Let \(I_{n}=\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\frac{\sin^{2}(nt)}{\sin t}dt\), find the largest integer smaller than \(1000 \times \lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{I_{n}}{\log_10{n}}\).
